title: Private VPC Egress Mesh + KV Cache Resilience Lab
summary: Deep technical session to validate egress topologies for a private VPC deployment, focus on PrivateLink vs NAT patterns, DNS/resolver behavior, KV cache hit resilience during NAT failover, and batching/quantization latency impacts. Agreed to run lab soak tests and exchange annotated network diagrams and performance results.
topics: PrivateLink endpoint placement and cross-account privatelink patterns
NAT gateway vs VPC egress proxy (hairpinning and connection tracking)
DNS resolvers, split-horizon, and stub resolver behaviour for subnet-level routing
KV cache warm/cold behavior during egress path changes
Batching/quantization tradeoffs on tail latency and GPU memory pressure
Mitigation strategies: connection draining, sticky routing, and bulk-prefetching KV keys

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-03-14, 16:00 UTC
Duration: 78 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Leah (Redwood SA), Priya (AcmeHealth Infra), Jamal (AcmeHealth Platform), Marta (AcmeHealth Security), Tom (AcmeHealth SRE)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be rough): Validate egress patterns for private VPC. Focus KV cache resiliency when NAT or PrivateLink path changes. Discussed DNS split-horizon, hairpin NAT, connection tracking, SNI/mTLS implications. Planned soak tests and network diagrams.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for jumping on, uh I think we've got about an hour and a quarter, so maybe we'll start with a quick context, Alex from Redwood, Samir is our runtime SE, Leah's our SA who will own the network diagrams.
[00:12] Priya: yeah thanks, quick context from our side, AcmeHealth has a HIPAA-adjacent workload, private VPC, we run in a multi-account setup, currently egress goes through a pair of NAT gateways in each AZ, there is also a central egress proxy for outbound inspection. We're trying to understand how Redwood's private deployment will behave if we move to PrivateLink endpoints for model traffic vs continuing with NAT + egress proxy. Our concerns are latency spikes, KV cache misses during failover and DNS behaviour.
[00:35] Samir: cool, that's exactly what we wanted to exercise. One note up front, our private plane—sorry private deployment uses client-initiated connections to a control plane for stats but runtime model traffic can stay entirely in your VPC, we'll show both patterns.
[00:48] Jamal: real quick, the thing we saw last week was when we cycled a NAT, a bunch of connections got reset and we saw KV cache hit rate drop from like 87% down to 32% and tail latency jumped, so we suspect connection tracking and ephemeral port churn is killing sticky sessions to GPU nodes.
[01:10] Samir: that makes sense. If the request path re-hashes you're going to go to a different runtime instance that doesn't have the same KV cache in RAM. So there are several levers: 1) Local KV replication/shard awareness 2) Sticky routing at LB or source IP preservation via PrivateLink 3) Prefetching hot KV keys on new instances when a cold miss is detected.
[01:38] Tom: can you elaborate on the PrivateLink option? we haven't set it up for cross-account, is it just an endpoint in each subnet?
[01:45] Leah: PrivateLink endpoints are ENIs in your subnet and you create a VPC endpoint service on our side. For cross-account you configure endpoint acceptance or use interface endpoints in the consumer account. The key is you preserve source IP and you avoid NAT hairpin which preserves TCP connections and therefore cache locality. But you need route table entries and security groups configured so that health checks and ephemeral ports are allowed.
[02:12] Marta: security question — how does this affect our audit logs and SAML flows? do we still get per-request audit IDs?
[02:18] Alex: yes — even for PrivateLink traffic we log token-level request IDs in the control plane and can stream audit logs to your S3/Kinesis. The only difference is where the wire hops occur; we still produce the same request metadata for tracing.
[02:33] Priya: ok, about DNS — we use an internal resolver in each VPC that returns private IPs for service names. If we switch to PrivateLink endpoints the resolver will hand back ENI IPs. But for failover if route tables change will the resolver cache TTLs cause us to keep hitting old IPs? we saw stale entries during a failover event last month.
[02:56] Samir: good point. DNS TTLs and client stub resolvers can cause delayed failover. We recommend low TTL for endpoint A records and using health checks plus route table automation to drain connections. For our runtime we also have a short-lived control plane mapping that the local agent uses to sanity check connectivity on connect, so it will detect immediate connectivity issues but won't necessarily fix staled OS resolver caches.
[03:20] Jamal: right, that explains why we had a window of about 30–90 seconds of errors. The other wrinkle is our egress proxy terminates TLS and reestablishes connections so from the runtime perspective the source IP changes.
[03:33] Samir: when there's TLS termination at the proxy you lose client IP hints unless you enable X-Forwarded-For and sticky session headers. That can also break our health-based routing heuristics. For KV cache we rely on consistent routing to keep hot keys colocated.
[03:50] Priya: what about using an egress NAT in combination with long-lived connections to the runtime? we could increase connection timeout and conn tracking table size.
[03:58] Samir: it's possible — increasing conntrack and ephemeral port ranges reduces churn but doesn't eliminate rehash if the path itself changes. NAT heals slower than PrivateLink but cheaper for some orgs.
[04:12] Leah: another middle ground is to run a local edge pod (sidecar) in each subnet that holds a tiny KV LRU cache and forwards requests to the backend; that reduces cross-AZ cache misses while keeping egress centralized for inspection. It adds operational overhead but often a good tradeoff.
[04:30] Tom: we'd prefer to avoid additional infra if possible, but sidecar sounds reasonable as a fallback. How does Redwood recommend cache sizing? our models have tokenized prompts that can produce tens of thousands of distinct KV keys.
[04:44] Samir: yes, prompts create a lot of keys. We usually recommend a two-tier policy: keep a hot set in memory (e.g., 50k keys depending on size) and use a secondary persistent cache—local SSD or memcached—for warm keys. Quantization reduces model memory but not KV footprint; quant profiles only change activations.
[05:03] Priya: you mentioned quantization — we do 4-bit quant on some models. any unexpected latency impact when quantized models are served across PrivateLink vs NAT?
[05:12] Samir: quantization typically reduces GPU memory and inference time, so network becomes relatively more dominant at low prompt sizes. If you're latency-bound, PrivateLink helps by reducing TCP teardown/reconnect penalties. Quantized models can also change batching behavior because each token is cheaper so throughput increases and you might want larger batch sizes; that affects tail latency tradeoffs.
[05:35] Jamal: curious about batching: we saw when batch size was bumped to 8 the 95p latency increased from 220ms to 480ms, but throughput improved by 2.8x. Any guidance?
[05:45] Samir: right — it's the classic latency vs cost/throughput trade. For interactive features we recommend dynamic batch windows with a hard latency cap and fast path for single-request flows. For background workloads you can maximize batch sizes. Also consider KV-aware batching: group requests likely to hit same cache shard to improve locality.
[06:08] Marta: from security we need mTLS to the endpoint plus SNI enforcement. Does PrivateLink preserve SNI?
[06:15] Leah: PrivateLink is L3/ENI-based, so TLS is end-to-end; SNI will be preserved. When you use an egress proxy that terminates TLS, SNI at our backend will show the proxy FQDN unless you pass the original via header. PrivateLink avoids that if you keep TLS passthrough.
[06:33] Tom: ok can we talk specifics: our current NAT setup uses 2 NAT gateways per AZ in an autoscaling pair, route tables point to a NAT in each private subnet. If we route to PrivateLink endpoints in each app subnet, are there limits on ENIs/endpoint count or ENI bandwidth we should watch?
[06:54] Leah: yes - interface endpoints create ENIs and each ENI has bandwidth limits. For extreme throughput, you want multiple endpoints per AZ and consider endpoint scaling. There's also an API rate limit for creation; so pre-provisioning is key. For high throughput we recommend using endpoint groups and spread across subnets to avoid single-ENI saturation.
[07:12] Priya: what about MTU? we run jumbo frames internally to improve throughput—does PrivateLink keep that or is there fragmentation?
[07:20] Samir: ENIs usually preserve MTU, but when traffic goes across certain AWS fabric or through proxies you can see path MTU differences. Test for fragmentation and adjust MSS clamping on edge NATs. We actually saw a 3–5% CPU increase when path MTU mismatch caused more fragmentation.
[07:38] Jamal: Leah, you mentioned connection draining earlier — can Redwood's runtime do graceful draining to preserve KV cache content on an instance being removed?
[07:45] Leah: yes our runtime supports graceful drain hooks. When an instance is being taken out we flush hot keys into a shared warmstore and signal the loadbalancer to stop new connections for a short period while ongoing requests finish. This reduces cold-miss storms but requires a warmstore to speed up new instance warmup.
[08:02] Tom: does that warmstore need to be in-region? we have regulatory constraints to keep data in-region for certain tenants.
[08:08] Alex: yes you can pin warmstore to region-local S3 or local SSD. For regulated workloads we recommend local encrypted warmstore with KMS integration.
[08:18] Priya: metrics — can we get token-level latency breakdown that includes connection setup, TLS handshake, app processing, and KV fetch time?
[08:26] Samir: absolutely, we emit span-level timing: DNS, TCP, TLS, request queuing, KV fetch, model infer, and token emission. You can map those to your dashboards and set alerts for KV miss spikes.
[08:38] Marta: quick compliance note — we need proof that traffic doesn't leave our VPC for certain tenants; with PrivateLink can you guarantee that?
[08:45] Alex: with PrivateLink, runtime workloads can run entirely inside your VPC and we can provide an on-prem package or a VPC Private deployment model that keeps all inference traffic internal. We'll document the data flow for your audit.
[08:58] Priya: ok, let's drill into the KV cache failover scenario we observed. Jamal, can you give the sequence?
[09:04] Jamal: sure. At T0 we rotated the NAT. Conntrack entries expired and new source ports were assigned; the loadbalancer rebalanced connections and about 20% of requests hit a different runtime host. Since that host didn't have the same KV segments, we saw a cascade of cold misses; cache TTLs were short so the miss storm lasted ~2 minutes while prefetch warmed things. During that window tail latency spiked to 1.2s from a baseline of 230ms.
[09:36] Samir: that lines up. Two immediate mitigations: increase TTLs for the hot keys and enable instance-to-instance warm propagation for hot keys during rotation. Also sticky sessioning via consistent hashing keyed on a request-level ID rather than source IP can reduce rehashes when NAT changes.
[09:54] Priya: consistent hashing — does Redwood's LB support that out of the box?
[09:58] Samir: yes we support hashing policies at the routing layer; you can hash on a token id we emit or your request id. We also support a fallback when the hashed host is unhealthy.
[10:08] Tom: curious about measuring 'hotness' — what's your recommended prefetch policy? we don't want to fetch 100k keys on instance start.
[10:16] Leah: start with LRU with a configurable hot-set threshold — keep the top 10% of most accessed keys computed over a rolling window. Add a short-lived amplification (fetch up to N keys synchronously on first miss) to prevent cascading misses. We can share a starter policy and example configs.
[10:33] Jamal: you mentioned earlier that proxy terminating TLS changes source IP. Any ways to preserve source identity through the proxy?
[10:39] Samir: yes — X-Forwarded-For and an authenticated header are common; you can also enable proxy protocol which preserves client IP to the backend. But your proxy must be trusted and enforce mTLS to avoid spoofing.
[10:52] Priya: about soak tests — we want to run a 1k qps test with intermittent NAT failover. Any recommendations on how to orchestrate it?
[10:58] Samir: orchestrate in phases: baseline run 10 minutes; introduce a NAT toggle at minute 12 (simulate failover) and leave for 5 minutes; then restore. Measure KV cache hit, 95/99 latencies, CPU/GPU util, conntrack table stats, and DNS cache metrics. We'll provide a test harness script to reproduce our recommendations.
[11:18] Tom: ok, can we instrument conntrack easily on our NAT? we're on managed NAT so limited access.
[11:24] Leah: if it's managed, you'll have CloudWatch metrics for active connections and you can augment with VPC flow logs (and use Athena to query). For per-packet details you need a NAT appliance where you can run conntrack.
[11:36] Marta: last security thing — if we do PrivateLink and keep TLS passthrough, how does token rotation and revocation work?
[11:44] Alex: tokens are short-lived and we support immediate revocation via control plane; since TLS is end-to-end the proxy can't replay tokens unless it's legitimately holding the TLS session keys. We also support per-request signing if you need extra assurance.
[11:56] Priya: any gotchas with cross-account privatelink acceptance automation? we have infra-as-code pipeline that should create endpoints; do we need manual acceptance steps?
[12:03] Leah: you can automate acceptance via API but some clouds require the service owner to accept; we can support pre-authorized principals to skip manual acceptance. We'll share example Terraform.
[12:18] Jamal: curious if Redwood has a recommended architecture for a hybrid mode — some tenants on PrivateLink, some via NAT.
[12:25] Samir: hybrid is common: tag tenants and route by tag. Use routing policies: latency-sensitive tenants -> PrivateLink; cost-sensitive -> NAT. The routing layer can fallback from PrivateLink to NAT if endpoints are saturated. Key is observability so you can track per-tenant KV miss rates.
[12:45] Priya: any bandwidth cost differences we should know about?
[12:49] Alex: PrivateLink has per-GB charges plus ENI costs; NAT has NAT gateway hourly and per-GB; in many cases PrivateLink is cheaper at scale but requires more ops. We'll run some cost examples with your traffic profile.
[13:05] Tom: okay, I think we have enough to run the lab, next steps?
[13:10] Alex: recap — Redwood to send annotated network diagram template, SOC2/security pack, and a test harness for the soak test. Acme to share subnet CIDRs, NAT config, proxy logs and pick tentative lab date. We'll follow up with the Terraform snippets for PrivateLink and endpoint pre-provisioning.
[13:30] Priya: sounds good. Thanks, everyone.
[13:33] Alex: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with dates — end meeting.
